newsitem.title: FRANCE: Road safety takes a back seat.
newsitem.headline: Road safety takes a back seat.

text.p: Motorists throughout the European Union will soon carry the same driving licence but differences between national legal systems means there will be no EU-wide ban on dangerous drivers.

The European Parliament on Wednesday reluctantly accepted there was insufficient support among EU governments for its demand that dangerous drivers who lose their licence in one EU member state be banned from driving throughout the Union.
National officials have been discussing mutual recognition of driving penalties for over eight years but legal and practical difficulties have blocked an agreement.

Faced with this impasse, Euro-MPs approved unamended a draft directive -- COM(96)55 -- which will harmonise the conditions under which motorists are authorised to drive in the EU, including minimum age and vision requirements, motoring skills and vehicle categories.

Their earlier demand -- that if member states could agree to a standard EU driving licence even though national driving tests differ, then they should also act together to reduce road deaths -- fell by the wayside after industry commissioner Martin Bangemann said the call was unlikely to receive the necessary unanimous support of all 15 EU governments.
Every year 50,000 people die on the Union's roads.
At present, motorists who commit offences in one EU country may continue to drive legally in the other 14.
If they commit an offence while in another member state, their licence is withdrawn only for as long as they remain in that country and is returned once they leave its territory.

If they are banned from driving in their home country, they can still apply for a licence in another member state, without necessarily having to inform that country's authorities of their earlier disqualification.
